name: Zoe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Pemberton family on Hightrees Farm, three hundred hectares of wheat and oilseed rape, and four hundred ewes. The family live in the city, so day to day it's me, two other workers and the farm agent who comes on Thursdays. I do the sheep, a lot of the tractor work, and two afternoons a week I do the farm office: the spray records, the sheep movements, the orders. I've been there twenty-two years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is lambing in the big shed, when it all goes right. Worst is February, when it's dark at both ends of the day and the spreadsheets don't add up. My husband Glen drives a grain lorry, so harvest is the one month we both barely see each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: handy in places, oversold in others. I use one of those AI assistants now and then for the spray records, and it saves me twenty minutes. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay good for us. The Pembertons pay fairly, Glen's work is steady, and My husband Glen and I have six payments left on the house, and that's the best feeling I've had in years. I'd be planning to stop at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Once the house is paid, I'd put that money into savings instead, about four hundred a month. And maybe use the AI assistant for the sheep movement forms too, since it's proven for the spray ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Pemberton children. When the old man goes, they might sell. But he's eighty-one and fit as a fiddle, so I don't lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra four hundred a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save most of it. Maybe a week in the sun with Glen once a year, which we haven't done since the kids left.

say: AI is **handy in places**, oversold in others.
It saves her about **twenty minutes** on the spray records, and that's all.
think: Things stay **good**: fair pay, Glen's steady work, and the **house** nearly paid.
do: Save about **£400 a month** once the house is paid.
Use the AI assistant for the **sheep movement** forms too.
S0.quote: My husband Glen and I have six payments left on the house, and that's the best feeling I've had in years.
fieldNote: Secure job, nearly **paid-off house** and a working partner: real calm.
Uses AI **now and then**, once it's proven on one task.
Her only distant worry is the owners' **children selling**.

steps.text: Save about £400 a month once the house mortgage ends
Use the AI assistant for sheep movement forms too
Keep working the sheep and tractor at Hightrees as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's in better shape than most, because so much is outside in the mud. I'd also say the office side will change fast. At the market I'd tell people to learn the new tools once they're settled, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my two office afternoons are the bit that goes. The agent would have software doing the orders and records by itself. The spreadsheets were the bit of my job I liked least, so I won't cry if software takes them. But I'd want those hours back as sheep work, not as a pay cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the agent before he comes to me and offer to run whatever system he picks. I'd do the short course the farm suppliers run on the new record software. And I'd ask for my hours to move to the sheep, since we're short there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, but not scared. It's my desk time, not my livelihood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the agent said no to moving your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose maybe a sixth of my pay, and we'd manage, with the house paid off. I'd still be cross about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at Hightrees would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody much, honestly. Dev and Paul are both hands-on, and they'd be fine for years.

Ask for her office hours to move to the **sheep**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and we should be honest about that. I'd say the people who own the land and the lorries will do fine, and the people who drive them won't. Not angrily, just plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one that touches both wages. My husband Glen drives a grain lorry and I drive a tractor, and both of those have a robot coming for them. The thinking side goes in 2028, the robots in 2031, and I'd be sixty-one then sixty-three. The Pembertons might keep one person to watch the machines, and I'd want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the agent this year that I want to be the one who runs the robots, and learn every system he brings in. I'd put the four hundred a month from the house into savings, every month. And I'd tell Glen to look at warehouse work at the grain store, which robots might reach later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a plan, but it depends on other people saying yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the three years between the thinking AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work's gone by 2028, so I'd be all sheep and tractor. Those three years are when I prove I'm useful with the new systems, before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Ella?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Ella, who's a vet nurse, that her job's safer than ours. She'd laugh, because she always said we should have done something with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people get going now, and I'd say it to the other workers at Hightrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to prove I'm the person who should be running the robots. Robots would come in 2034, when I'm sixty-six and stopping anyway. Glen's a year younger, so he'd be close too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a proper course on farm robotics at the college over two winters. I'd keep saving the house money. And I'd tell the agent I'd stay a year past sixty-six if he wanted someone to train the young ones on the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fine. It's tight, but the dates mostly work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really stay past sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, if the money's right. I'd like to hand over properly, not just walk off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Glen think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Glen says he'll drive until the lorry drives itself, and then he'll take up fishing. He means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should use it. The young ones especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, this one's easy. I retire at sixty-six in 2034, and Glen soon after. Robots in 2039 are someone else's worry, and I'd tell the young ones to start on them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Hightrees, keep saving, and retire on time. I'd learn whatever the agent brings in, as I always do. I'd tell Josh, our son in the army, to get a trade he can take anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a long forecast with sun at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything here that bothers you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only what happens to Hightrees. I'd like it still to be a farm with people on it, but that's not my decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Josh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Josh to learn to fix the robots in the army, for free, and then walk out into a good job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Glen and I both drive for a living and both get hit by 2031. What would help is an employer who'd keep one experienced person on to run the machines, and a bit of help bridging to our pensions.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want to run robots. I would, actually. I'd rather be the person who knows the machines than the person they replaced.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the person who knows the machines than the person they replaced.
portrait: Zoe, **58**, works the sheep, tractor and **farm office** on a family-owned arable and sheep farm.
Her husband Glen drives a **grain lorry**, and their house is nearly **paid off**.
She uses AI **now and then** and moves once a tool is proven.
Fast AGI puts **both wages** at risk, so she aims to run the robots herself.
With five or ten years, the dates line up with **retirement** and she stays calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both she and Glen **drive** for a living.
whatWouldHelp: An employer keeping **one experienced person** to run the machines.
